title: Business Delegate Pattern
oneLiner: Shields client code from the complexity and volatility of looking up and calling remote business services, behind a simple local stand-in.

hero.name: The Envoy
hero.catchphrase: You don't talk to the business tier directly. Send it through me.
hero.power: Shields client code from remote service lookup and networking complexity, presenting a simple, local, stable interface instead.
hero.weakness: A very J2EE-era pattern, largely superseded by simpler modern remoting and DI approaches — reaching for it in a modern stack can be unnecessary ceremony.
hero.origin: The Envoy appeared after a client-tier UI class had raw JNDI lookup code, remote-exception handling, and retry logic directly inside its button-click handler, just to call one business method.

story.problem: A UI button handler contains raw JNDI lookup code, remote-exception handling, and retry logic, just to call one method on a remote business service. Every screen that calls the business tier repeats this same plumbing.
story.solution: The Envoy introduces an `OrderServiceDelegate` that hides the JNDI lookup, exception translation, and retries behind one simple method: `placeOrder()`. UI code calls that, and nothing else.
story.result: UI code no longer touches JNDI, remote exceptions, or retry logic at all. Every screen that needs the business tier just calls the delegate's simple methods.

before: Client code directly performs remote service lookups
Remote exception handling is duplicated across every call site
A change to the lookup mechanism ripples through client code everywhere
after: Client code calls one simple, local delegate method
Remote exception handling and retries live in one place
A change to the lookup mechanism only touches the delegate

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A UI button handler has raw JNDI lookup code and retry logic mixed directly into its click event.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Every single screen that calls the order service repeats this same JNDI lookup and retry boilerplate. It's everywhere.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Envoy appears, offering to carry every message to the business tier so the client never has to reach it directly.
panels.speaker: The Envoy
panels.dialogue: Stop reaching into the business tier yourself. Send your requests through me — I'll handle the lookup, the retries, all of it.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: OrderServiceDelegate.placeOrder() hides JNDI lookup, exception translation, and retry logic behind one simple call.
panels.speaker: The Envoy
panels.dialogue: UI code just calls placeOrder(). All the remoting complexity — lookup, retries, exception translation — lives inside me, not in every button handler.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Every screen now calls one simple delegate method, with zero JNDI code in sight.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Every screen just calls placeOrder() now. Not one of them touches JNDI or retry logic directly anymore.

useWhen: You're working with a genuinely heavyweight remote service lookup mechanism (classic JNDI/EJB-style systems) that shouldn't leak into client code.
Multiple client-tier screens or components need to call the same remote business services and shouldn't duplicate lookup/retry logic.
You want a stable local interface that insulates clients from changes in how the business tier is actually reached.
avoidWhen: You're on a modern stack where simple HTTP clients, gRPC stubs, or dependency injection already provide this insulation without extra ceremony.
There's no real remoting complexity to hide — a plain function call or lightweight SDK client is already simple enough.
The added indirection doesn't map to any actual pain point your team has experienced.
commonMistakes: Applying Business Delegate to modern, already-simple remoting (a REST client, a typed gRPC stub) where it adds ceremony without solving a real problem — this is a very J2EE-era pattern.
Letting the delegate leak low-level remoting exceptions back to client code anyway, defeating the point of the abstraction.
Not caching the expensive lookup when appropriate, repeating costly service discovery on every single call.
Confusing Business Delegate with Facade — Business Delegate specifically targets remote/business-tier lookup complexity; Facade simplifies access to any complex subsystem, remote or not.
explanation.realWorldExample: Classic Java EE applications using Business Delegate to wrap EJB lookups behind a simple client-tier interface are the textbook use case — modern equivalents include typed API client wrappers that hide authentication, retries, and endpoint discovery behind simple method calls.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this the same as a typical typed API client we'd write today?

conversation.speaker: The Envoy
conversation.message: Spiritually, very close! Modern SDK wrappers hiding auth, retries, and endpoint discovery are doing exactly what I was invented for — just without the specific J2EE/EJB baggage I originally carried.

conversation.speaker: The Envoy
conversation.message: By that specific name, mostly, yes. But the underlying idea — insulate clients from remote-lookup complexity — is alive and well in every well-designed API client wrapper written today.

codeBattle.scenario: Your legacy enterprise Java application has EJB lookup code, connection retries, and remote exception translation duplicated across fifteen different client-tier screens that all need to call the same business service.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Envoy centralizes the EJB lookup, retry, and exception-translation logic behind one simple delegate interface, so the fifteen screens stop duplicating remoting plumbing.

quiz.question: What does Business Delegate shield client code from?
options: The complexity and volatility of looking up and calling remote business services
The need to have any business logic at all
quiz.answer: The complexity and volatility of looking up and calling remote business services
quiz.explanation: Insulating clients from remote lookup and networking details is exactly what this pattern exists to do.

quiz.question: What era/technology is Business Delegate classically associated with?
options: Classic Java EE applications using EJB lookups
quiz.answer: Classic Java EE applications using EJB lookups
quiz.explanation: Business Delegate is a well-known J2EE-era pattern, originally designed around hiding EJB lookup complexity.

quiz.question: What's the modern equivalent of what Business Delegate provides?
options: A typed API client wrapper hiding authentication, retries, and endpoint discovery behind simple method calls
A raw HTTP fetch call with no abstraction
quiz.answer: A typed API client wrapper hiding authentication, retries, and endpoint discovery behind simple method calls
quiz.explanation: The underlying idea persists in modern SDK/API client wrappers, even without the specific EJB-era name.

quiz.question: How does Business Delegate differ from Facade?
options: Business Delegate specifically targets remote/business-tier lookup complexity; Facade simplifies access to any complex subsystem
They are the exact same pattern with different names
Facade can only be used for remote services
Business Delegate requires a NoSQL database
quiz.answer: Business Delegate specifically targets remote/business-tier lookup complexity; Facade simplifies access to any complex subsystem
quiz.explanation: Business Delegate is a more specific application of simplification, focused on remote service access rather than any subsystem in general.
